t.4.22.1: Gazing all around, his life-breath faint and breathing slowly, he first of all beheld Sugrīva standing before his own son.
t.4.22.2: Vālī addressed Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, who had won the victory, and in a clear voice spoke these words to him with affection.
t.4.22.3: O Sugrīva, you should not hold me guilty for my offence, for I was dragged along by force by a delusion of the mind that fate had ordained.
t.4.22.5: Take up, this very day, the kingship of these forest-dwellers, and know that I too, this very day, am going to the abode of Vaivasvata.
t.4.22.4: Dear one, I do not think that happiness was ordained for the two of us at the same time, for the affection that befits brothers has turned out otherwise.
t.4.22.6: Indeed, I am now swiftly giving up my life, my kingdom, this vast prosperity, and my great and unblemished fame.
t.4.22.8: Look at Aṅgada, this boy who is no fool, deserving of comfort and raised in comfort, lying fallen on the ground, his face filled with tears.
t.4.22.7: But in this state, O hero, whatever words I shall speak, even if it is hard, O king, you ought indeed to carry it out.
t.4.22.9: My son, dearer to me than my own life, who will be bereft of me though he lacks nothing, protect him in every way as if he were your own son born of your body.
t.4.22.10: For you too, O lord of the monkeys, are his provider and his protector on every side, and the giver of fearlessness amid dangers, just as I am.
t.4.22.12: This Aṅgada, son of Tārā, young, swift and mighty, will display his valour in battle and perform deeds worthy of himself.
t.4.22.11: This glorious son of Tārā, equal to you in valour, will stand at your forefront in the slaying of those Rākṣasas.
t.4.22.13: And this daughter of Suṣeṇa is fully accomplished in every respect, both in determining the subtle meaning of matters and in interpreting the various kinds of portents.
t.4.22.14: Whatever she declares to be good must be done without any doubt, for nothing that Tārā has judged ever turns out otherwise.
t.4.22.15: And Rāghava's task must be carried out by you without hesitation, for there would be unrighteousness in failing to do it, and he, if slighted, might kill you.
t.4.22.16: And put on this divine golden garland, O Sugrīva, for the exalted glory that abides in it would abandon it once I am dead.
t.4.22.17: Thus addressed by Vālin out of brotherly affection, Sugrīva cast off his joy and became dejected once more, like the king of stars seized by the eclipsing planet.
t.4.22.18: Then, at Vālin's words, he grew calm and, alert and doing what was fitting, took that golden garland once he had been given leave.
t.4.22.19: Having given away that golden garland, Vālin, fully prepared for his existence after death, saw his son standing there and spoke with affection to Aṅgada.
t.4.22.20: Adapt yourself now to place and time, bearing with patience both the pleasant and the unpleasant; enduring joy and sorrow as they come in time, remain under the authority of Sugrīva.
t.4.22.21: Mighty-armed one, you have always been indulged by me, but Sugrīva will not hold you in such high regard if you go on behaving as you did with me.
t.4.22.22: Do not follow the path taken by his enemies, nor that of my foes, O tamer of enemies. Devoted to your master's welfare and self-restrained, remain under Sugrīva's command.
t.4.22.23: You should not show excessive affection, nor should you show a lack of affection, for both are a great fault; therefore be one who keeps to the middle way.
t.4.22.24: Having spoken thus, his eyes rolling, grievously tormented by the arrow, with his dreadful teeth laid bare, he then breathed his last.
t.4.22.25: When the heroic lord of the monkeys had been slain, the monkeys there found no peace, just as forest-roaming cows find none in a great forest filled with lions when the lord of the herd has been killed.
t.4.22.26: Then Tārā, plunged into an ocean of calamity, gazed upon the face of her dead husband and, embracing Vālin, sank to the ground like a creeper clinging to a great tree that has been cut down.
